summary: This memo describes how to run SNMP over the OSI connectionless-mode transport service, for networks that use OSI protocols instead of UDP and IP. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines how to carry SNMP messages over the OSI connectionless-mode transport service. It is intended for networks where UDP is unavailable, and the memo identifies UDP as the preferred mapping.

questions: what are the snmp transport selectors for osi
how big can an snmp message be over osi
what minimum message size must snmp over osi accept
subtitle: Mapping SNMP onto the OSI connectionless-mode transport service.

tldr.problem: Sites with OSI capabilities may want to use SNMP to manage OSI components where UDP transport is unavailable.
tldr.mechanism: The memo maps SNMP onto the OSI connectionless-mode transport service and defines transport selectors for requests and traps.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1418 obsoletes RFCs 1161 and 1283 and has Historic status. The memo says UDP remains the preferred SNMP mapping.

today: RFC 1418 has Historic status and obsoletes RFC 1161 and RFC 1283. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 1418.

sections.title: Why Map SNMP to OSI
sections.content:
The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) is used in the management framework for TCP/IP networks. Sites with OSI capabilities may want to use their SNMP technology to manage OSI components.

This memo defines a framework for running SNMP over the OSI connectionless-mode transport service (CLTS). It states that UDP is the preferred mapping and that this specification is for environments where UDP is unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo describes an SNMP transport for OSI networks. It says the mapping is intended for places that cannot use UDP.

sections.title: Transport Addresses and Selectors
sections.content:
The procedures for mapping SNMP onto the CLTS are identical to those for UDP. A transport address consists of a transport selector and a network address. OSI does not use well-known ports; it uses selectors, which are opaque strings of octets with local significance.

For a connectionless-mode network service, the SNMP selector is snmp-l and the trap selector is snmpt-l. For a connection-oriented network service, they are snmp-o and snmpt-o.
sections.plainLanguage: OSI uses selector strings instead of well-known ports for this mapping. The RFC gives one selector for SNMP and one for traps for each service type.

sections.title: Traps and Message Size
sections.content:
For a trap sent over the CLTS, the agent-addr field in the Trap-PDU contains the IP address 0.0.0.0. A manager may determine the trap source from information supplied by the transport service.

An SNMP-over-OSI entity must be prepared to accept messages of at least 484 octets. Implementations are encouraged to support larger sizes when possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The trap message uses 0.0.0.0 in its agent address field, and the manager can use transport information to identify the source. Receivers must accept messages of at least 484 octets.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that security issues are not discussed in this memo. It defines transport mapping details but provides no security analysis of the mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security issues for this transport mapping.
